table.caption: Selected values of a twice-differentiable function f. Also, f''(x) > 0 for 1.5 ≤ x ≤ 2.5 and f''(x) < 0 for 4.5 ≤ x ≤ 5.5.

local-linearity-s2.title: The graph of $y = \ln x$ and its tangent line at $x = 1$

plot.label: Graph of y = ln x for x from 0.2 to 4, with the dashed tangent line y = x - 1 touching it at (1, 0) and lying above it elsewhere

items.q: Using the table, write the linearization $L(x)$ of $f$ at $x = 2$, in the form $y = \ldots$

mistakes.why: The value $f(2) = 5$ is the starting height and $f'(2) = -3$ is the slope; they are swapped.
The slope is $f'(2) = -3$, so the term is $-3(x - 2)$.

why.correct: The point is $(2, f(2)) = (2, 5)$ and the slope is $f'(2) = -3$: $L(x) = 5 - 3(x - 2)$.

items.q: Use the tangent line at $x = 2$ to approximate $f(2.1)$.

mistakes.why: Multiply the slope by the change $x - 2 = 0.1$, not by $x = 2.1$.

items.q: Is the approximation of $f(2.1)$ from the tangent line an overestimate or an underestimate?
options: An underestimate, because $f'' > 0$ makes $f$ concave up there
An overestimate, because $f'(2) < 0$
An overestimate, because $f'' > 0$ there
Neither: the tangent line gives the exact value of $f(2.1)$

why.correct: On $1.5 \le x \le 2.5$, $f'' > 0$, so the graph is concave up and lies above the tangent line. $L(2.1)$ is below $f(2.1)$: an underestimate.
options: A concave up graph lies above its tangent lines.
The sign of $f'$ says which way the line slopes, not which side of the graph it lies on.
Concave up puts the tangent line below the graph, giving an underestimate.
The line matches $f$ only at $x = 2$; elsewhere the graph bends away from it.

items.q: Use the line tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x = 5$ to approximate $f(4.8)$.

mistakes.why: That uses the tangent line at $x = 2$: $5 - 3(2.8) = -3.4$. That point is far from 4.8; use the closest one, $x = 5$.

items.q: Is the approximation of $f(4.8)$ an overestimate or an underestimate?
options: An underestimate, because $f'' < 0$ there
An overestimate, because $f'' < 0$ makes $f$ concave down there
An underestimate, because 4.8 lies to the left of the point $x = 5$
An overestimate, because $f'(5) > 0$

why.correct: On $4.5 \le x \le 5.5$, $f'' < 0$: concave down, so the tangent line lies above the graph and $L(4.8)$ overestimates $f(4.8)$.
options: Concave down puts the tangent line above the graph.
A concave down graph lies below its tangent lines.
The side of the point does not matter; the concavity does.
The sign of $f'$ does not decide; the reason must be about $f''$.

items.q: Use the tangent line shown to approximate $\ln(1.2)$.

mistakes.why: The line is $y = x - 1$, not $y = x$: $L(1.2) = 1.2 - 1$.

why.correct: The tangent line at $(1, 0)$ has slope $\frac{1}{1} = 1$: $L(x) = x - 1$, so $\ln(1.2) \approx 0.2$.

items.q: Is $0.2$ an overestimate or an underestimate of $\ln(1.2)$?
options: An underestimate, because $\ln x$ is increasing on its whole domain
An underestimate, because $\ln(1.2) > 0$
An overestimate, because the graph of $\ln x$ is concave down
An overestimate, because $1.2 > 1$

why.correct: The second derivative of $\ln x$ is $-\frac{1}{x^2} < 0$: the graph is concave down and lies below its tangent line, so $L(1.2) = 0.2$ is too large.
options: Increasing does not decide which side the tangent line is on.
Both numbers are positive; compare them using concavity.
Concave down: the tangent line lies above the curve, as the graph shows.
Points on either side of 1 give overestimates here; the reason is the concavity.

items.q: The same tangent line is used to approximate $\ln(1.2)$ and $\ln(3)$. Which approximation is more accurate?
options: $\ln(3)$, because the line and the curve both grow
They are equally accurate, since the same line is used
Neither, since a tangent line gives no information away from $x = 1$
$\ln(1.2)$, because 1.2 is closer to the point of tangency

why.correct: Local linearity: close to the point of tangency the graph looks like the line. $L(1.2) = 0.2$ versus $\ln 1.2 \approx 0.182$; $L(3) = 2$ versus $\ln 3 \approx 1.099$.
options: The graph shows the gap widening as $x$ moves away from 1.
The error depends on how far $x$ is from the point of tangency.
Close to $x = 1$ it gives good estimates.
Near $x = 1$ the curve and the line almost coincide; at $x = 3$ they are far apart.

items.q: Write the linear approximation of $\ln x$ at $x = e$, in the form $y = \ldots$

mistakes.why: The slope of $\ln x$ at $x = e$ is $\frac{1}{e}$, not $e$.
Start from the height $\ln e = 1$ at the point of tangency.

why.correct: $\ln e = 1$ and the slope is $\frac{1}{e}$: $L(x) = 1 + \frac{1}{e}(x - e)$.

items.q: Use a tangent line approximation of $\sqrt{x}$ at $x = 25$ to estimate $\sqrt{26}$.

mistakes.why: The derivative of $\sqrt{x}$ is $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$: at 25 that is $\frac{1}{10}$, not $\frac{1}{5}$.
The slope multiplies the change in $x$, which is 1, and the slope is $\frac{1}{10}$, not 1.

items.q: Is the estimate $\sqrt{26} \approx 5.1$ too large or too small, and why?
options: Too large, because $\sqrt{x}$ is concave down
Too small, because $\sqrt{x}$ is increasing
Too small, because 26 is greater than 25
Too small, because the slope $\frac{1}{10}$ is positive

why.correct: $\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\sqrt{x} = -\frac{1}{4}x^{-3/2} < 0$: concave down, tangent line above the graph, so 5.1 is an overestimate.
options: The second derivative $-\frac{1}{4}x^{-3/2}$ is negative.
Increasing does not decide; concavity does.
The direction of the step does not decide; concavity does.
A positive slope tells which way the line rises, not which side of the graph it is on.

items.q: Use the tangent line to $f(x) = x^{10}$ at $x = 1$ to approximate $(1.02)^{10}$.

mistakes.why: The slope is $f'(1) = 10$; the step 0.02 is multiplied by 10.

items.q: The tangent line to $y = \sin x$ at $x = 0$ gives $\sin(0.1) \approx 0.1$. Which is true?
options: $0.1$ is an underestimate, because $\sin x$ is concave up near 0
$0.1$ is an overestimate, because $\sin x$ is concave down on $(0, \pi)$
$0.1$ is exact, because the tangent line is $y = x$
$0.1$ is an overestimate, because $\cos 0 = 1$

why.correct: $L(x) = x$ at 0. On $(0, \pi)$, $\sin x$ is concave down, so the line lies above it and $0.1 > \sin 0.1$.
options: For $0 < x < \pi$, $\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\sin x = -\sin x < 0$.
The second derivative $-\sin x$ is negative there.
$\sin x$ and $x$ agree only at 0; $\sin 0.1 \approx 0.0998$.
The slope at 0 gives the line; whether it is above the curve depends on concavity.

items.q: Use the tangent line to $y = e^x$ at $x = 0$ to approximate $e^{0.1}$.

mistakes.why: That is the value at $x = 0$; add the slope times the step, $1 \times 0.1$.

why.correct: $e^0 = 1$ and the slope is $e^0 = 1$: $L(x) = 1 + x$, so $e^{0.1} \approx 1.1$.

items.q: If the graph of $f$ is concave up on an interval containing $x = a$, the line tangent to the graph at $x = a$
options: lies above the graph near $a$, so it overestimates $f(x)$
crosses the graph at $x = a$
lies below the graph near $a$, so it underestimates $f$
gives exact values near $a$

why.correct: Concave up: the graph bends upward, away from the tangent line, so the line lies below it and tangent line approximations are underestimates.
options: That happens when the graph is concave down.
With constant concavity, the graph stays on one side of its tangent line near $a$.
Concave up graphs bend up away from their tangent lines.
It matches $f$ exactly only at $x = a$.

items.q: A function has $f(3) = 2$, $f'(3) = 0.5$ and $f''(x) < 0$ for all $x$. Which is true about the tangent line approximation of $f(3.4)$?
options: It is $2.2$, an underestimate
It is $2.5$, an overestimate
It is $1.8$, an overestimate
It is $2.2$, an overestimate

why.correct: $L(3.4) = 2 + 0.5(0.4) = 2.2$. Since $f'' < 0$, the graph is concave down and below the tangent line, so 2.2 is too large.
options: With $f'' < 0$ the graph lies below its tangent lines.
Multiply the slope by the step $0.4$: $0.5(0.4) = 0.2$.
The slope is positive, so the estimate rises from 2.
$2 + 0.5(0.4) = 2.2$; concave down puts the line above the graph.
